topic: Do You Need a Dummy Ticket for a US Visa Interview?
metaTitle: Do You Need a Dummy Ticket for a US Visa Interview?
metaDescription: A dummy ticket is not required for a B1/B2 interview. Here is what the DS-160 asks, what the officer is really assessing, and where a reservation helps.
excerpt: A B1/B2 interview is decided on intent, not on the documents in your folder. This guide covers what the DS-160 asks about your travel plans, what a consular officer is actually weighing, and the narrow situations where a flight reservation is worth having.
quickAnswer: No, a dummy ticket is not a required document for a B1/B2 interview. The State Department lists the DS-160 confirmation page, a passport and a photograph as the essentials, and says supporting documents are only requested to show your purpose, your ability to pay and your intent to depart. A reservation speaks to that last point and to nothing else.
content:
No. A dummy ticket is not on the list of documents you have to bring to a B1/B2 interview, and no consular officer will turn you away for arriving without one. The interview turns on intent, not paperwork. The officer is deciding whether you will go home again, and that means a flight reservation is useful in one narrow way and completely beside the point in several others.

Do you need a dummy ticket for a US visa interview?

No, it is not required. The US Department of State's visitor visa guidance puts the DS-160 confirmation page, a valid passport and a photograph in the category of things you must have. Everything beyond that is a supporting document, and supporting documents are requested, not mandatory.

Where a reservation earns its place is in one of the three categories the State Department names. An officer may ask for evidence of the purpose of your trip, your intent to depart the United States after it, and your ability to pay all costs. A booking that shows your name, a route and a date you leave again speaks to the second one.

It does nothing about the other two. If the officer is not convinced about your funds or your ties to the UAE, a held reservation is noise in the file.

At a glance: flight reservations and the B1/B2 interview

Is a flight booking a required document?No. The required items are the DS-160 confirmation page, a passport and a photograph. Supporting documents are optionalUS Department of State
What can an officer ask you to evidence?The purpose of the trip, your intent to depart the United States afterwards, and your ability to pay all costs of the tripUS Department of State
What is the legal starting point?Every applicant is presumed to be an intending immigrant until they establish eligibility for nonimmigrant status, under section 214(b)9 FAM 403.10, Foreign Affairs Manual
Does an invitation letter help?It is not needed. Applicants qualify on their own residence and ties abroad rather than on assurances from family or friends in the United StatesUS Department of State
Is an itinerary useful on the DS-160?Yes, the form's own guidance says a travel itinerary may be useful if you have already made travel arrangementsDS-160 frequently asked questions
Can you interview in the UAE?Check before you plan anything. The Mission's visa page has said routine visa processing is not available in the UAE, and applicants have been pointed to the post in their country of nationality or residenceUS Mission to the United Arab Emirates
Is a ticket ever actually required?Yes, but not for a visa. Travellers arriving under the Visa Waiver Programme by air or sea need a return or onward ticketUS Department of State

What does the DS-160 actually ask about your travel plans?

Less than people expect. The travel section wants your intended date of arrival, how long you plan to stay, the address where you will be staying and who is paying for the trip. None of those fields require a purchased fare.

You are allowed to say your plans are not finalised. Plenty of approved applicants do, because a sensible person does not buy a long-haul ticket before a stranger has decided whether they can board the plane.

The State Department's DS-160 guidance puts it in the useful column rather than the required one: have a travel itinerary to hand if you have already made arrangements. If you have not, answer with your intended dates and keep them consistent with everything else in the file.

One mechanical point that catches people out. The appointment is tied to the barcode on your DS-160 confirmation page, so the form you submit and the form you booked with have to be the same one. Fill in a fresh DS-160 after booking and you can find yourself rebooking the appointment too.

What does the consular officer actually want to see?

A reason to believe you are coming back. That is the whole interview, and it usually lasts a couple of minutes.

The Foreign Affairs Manual is blunt about the starting position. Every visa applicant is presumed to be an immigrant until the applicant satisfies the officer otherwise. You are not proving you have the right documents. You are displacing a legal presumption with your own circumstances.

The State Department describes those circumstances as ties, meaning the parts of your life that bind you to the country you live in: a job, a home, family, commitments that are waiting for you. The same manual adds a caution worth repeating, that section 214(b) does not simply mean an applicant must have ties, because a refusal can also reflect not meeting the requirements of the visa category itself.

Nationality matters here more than most people are told. A UAE resident on an Indian, Pakistani or Egyptian passport is assessed on the ties they hold in the UAE and at home, and a residence visa with two years left on it reads differently from one expiring next month.

Does a flight reservation help or hurt your case?

It helps in a small, specific way, and it is honest to say the way is small. A verifiable booking lets your answers and your file agree with each other. If you tell the officer you are going for ten days in March, a reservation on the table says the same thing in the same words.

It is also the easier half of a business trip. Where an employer letter names dates for a conference or a client meeting, a matching reservation makes the trip look planned rather than theoretical, which is the point the B-1 category is about.

That is why we sell a flight reservation for a B1/B2 file rather than a visa service. It is a genuine airline booking held under a live PNR, which means it can be looked up in Amadeus, Sabre or Travelport like any other reservation. It is not a forged document and it is not a paid ticket, and you should never present it as one.

Where it hurts is when it is doing a job it cannot do. A reservation attached to a thin application does not rescue it. If the concern is that your salary does not support the trip, or that you have little holding you in the UAE, or that a previous refusal has not been answered, the booking changes nothing at all. Say the quiet part out loud: on those questions the document is irrelevant.

What should you take to a B1/B2 interview?

Keep it tight. Officers work through a queue and read what they ask for.

  • Your passport, valid for at least six months beyond your intended stay in the United States, plus your old passports if you have them
  • The printed DS-160 confirmation page, with the barcode that matches your appointment
  • Your appointment confirmation letter
  • One recent photograph to the published specification, taken in the last six months
  • Your visa fee receipt, where the post you are applying at asks for it before the interview
  • Your Emirates ID and residence visa, as evidence of where you actually live
  • Proof of employment and income: an employer letter, recent pay slips, bank statements covering the trip
  • A dummy ticket for your US visa appointment or any booking you have already made, if you want the travel plan on paper
  • Any document the trip itself depends on, such as a conference registration, a hospital appointment or a business invitation

Note what is not on that list. The visitor visa guidance says a letter of invitation or an affidavit of support is not needed, because you qualify on your residence and ties abroad rather than on what someone in the United States promises about you.

Why are B1/B2 applications actually refused?

Almost never for a missing reservation. The refusals happen for reasons that have nothing to do with the folder you carry in.

  • The presumption stands. Most refusals under section 214(b) happen because the applicant did not convince the officer of an intent to return abroad. There is no appeal and no waiver for it.
  • The story does not hold together. A DS-160 that says two weeks, an answer at the window that says a month, and a hotel booking that says something else again. Consistency is doing more work than any single document.
  • The money is unexplained. If the trip costs more than your income plausibly covers, the officer will ask who is paying. A balance that appeared in your account last week invites the question rather than answering it.
  • The ties are thin. A short-notice job, no property, no dependants and a residence visa close to expiry is a harder set of facts, and no booking changes any of them.
  • Reapplying with nothing new. The State Department asks for evidence of significant changes in circumstances since the last application. A fresh reservation is not a changed circumstance.
  • Treating documents as the case. Supporting documents support answers. They do not replace them, and a thick folder can read as anxiety rather than evidence.

Should you buy the flight before the decision?

No, and this is the part that costs people real money. A refusal under section 214(b) comes with no appeal, no waiver and no refund of the application fee, which is payable whether a visa is issued or not. Add a non-refundable Dubai to New York fare on top of that and a two minute conversation turns into a four figure loss.

The sensible order is to put the plan on paper, attend the interview, and buy the fare once the passport comes back with the visa in it. That is the entire reason a reservation for a US visa application exists as a product: it holds the shape of the trip without you betting on the outcome.

Applying from the UAE adds its own reason to wait. The Mission's own visa page has carried notices about routine processing being unavailable here and applicants being directed to the post in their country of nationality or residence, with interview slots released on a weekly cycle. That position has moved more than once this year, so read the page on the day rather than trusting what a forum told you last month. If your interview ends up being in Delhi, Islamabad or Cairo, the flight you need first is that one.

What does it cost?

Two separate bills, and it is worth seeing them apart. Ours buys a document. The government's buys a decision, and it does not care which way the decision goes.

So what should you do before your interview?

Spend your effort on the answers, not the folder. Know your dates, know who is paying, know what you are going back to in the UAE, and be able to say all three in a sentence each without reaching for a document.

Then, if you want the travel plan written down in a form the officer can read in two seconds, book the reservation and print it. It is a supporting document doing a supporting document's job, which is the honest size of it.

faqs.question: Is a dummy ticket required for a US visa interview?
faqs.answer: No. The required items are your DS-160 confirmation page, passport and photograph. The State Department treats a flight booking as an optional supporting document, useful for showing you intend to leave the United States again and nothing more.

faqs.question: Will a flight reservation improve my chances of approval?
faqs.answer: Only slightly, and only on one point. It helps your dates stay consistent and shows a planned trip. If the officer's doubt is about your funds or your ties to the UAE, the booking changes nothing, because no document decides a B1/B2 case.

faqs.question: Can I complete the DS-160 without booking a flight?
faqs.answer: Yes. The travel section asks for your intended arrival date, how long you plan to stay, where you will stay and who is paying. You can state intended dates and say plans are not finalised. The official guidance calls an itinerary useful, not required.

faqs.question: Should I buy my ticket before the visa is approved?
faqs.answer: No. A refusal under section 214(b) has no appeal and no waiver, and the application fee is not refunded. Hold the plan with a reservation from AED 49, attend the interview, then buy the fare once the visa is in your passport.

faqs.question: Can I interview for a US visa in Dubai or Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Check the Mission's visa page on the day. Notices have said routine visa processing is not available in the UAE and have pointed applicants to the post in their country of nationality or residence. The position has changed more than once this year.
